title: Incident bridging workshop — VelaHealth follow-up
summary: Follow-up bridgecall after Friday's production cascade. Reviewed postmortem hypotheses (KV cache pressure, backpressure on the dedicated pool, and a routing fallback misconfiguration), aligned on immediate mitigations and runbook edits, agreed to a shared repro window for the SE+SRE teams, and scheduled a dedicated benchmarking session for the customer's burst profile.
next_steps: Jordan to share annotated runbook and throttling recommendations by 2026-08-20
Maya + Sofia to run repro during shared window and confirm root cause by 2026-08-21
Schedule 2-hour benchmarking session with dedicated capacity mock on 2026-08-25
Provide security artifact set (SOC2/ISO) for Liam by 2026-08-22
action_items: Jordan Price — Send annotated runbook (include circuit-breaker thresholds, cache TTL tuning) — due 2026-08-20
Maya Chen — Run KV-cache stress repro with VelaHealth dataset and share logs — due 2026-08-21
Sofia Ramos — Provide request traces and pre/post-incident traffic spike CSVs — due 2026-08-19
Liam O'Connor — Approve on-prem test window and sign NDA for dataset mirror — due 2026-08-21
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-18   Time: 16:00 UTC   Duration: ~52m
Attendees: Jordan Price (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Amir Patel (VelaHealth Platform), Sofia Ramos (VelaHealth SRE Lead), Liam O'Connor (VelaHealth CTO)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick intros — I'm Jordan, AE. Maya from our infra team is here — she'll drive the repro and the technical next steps.
[00:09] Amir: Hi all, Amir here. Thanks for setting this up. Sofia will fill in most of the SRE detail.
[00:15] Sofia: Hi — thanks. We had a rough Friday and want to make sure the path forward is clear.
[00:22] Maya: Yep. Couple goals for today: confirm the top hypotheses from the postmortem, align on immediate mitigations we can push without a deploy, and set a repro + bench cadence. Also any security asks.
[00:33] Liam: That's great. For context, exec wants clear remediation and an ask for cost implications if we move to dedicated pool vs sticking hosted.

[02:10] Jordan: Quick recap — our postmortem draft identified three likely contributors: KV cache pressure leading to long tail miss amplification, aggressive prefetch/batching behavior on long requests, and a misrouted fallback that sent traffic to a lower-tier model unexpectedly. Maya, feel free to correct the wording.
[02:29] Maya: Yeah that's right. The logs show two things in particular — a spike in cache miss ratio around the time windows, and the serving layer starting to batch older requests together which increased latency; then routing kicked to a cheaper variant that wasn't warm, which exacerbated queueing.
[02:45] Sofia: On our side the SLO alerts were mostly token-queue growth and connection retries. We also saw backend retries from the integration layer which multiplied traffic to the inference endpoints.

[05:00] Amir: We flagged an operational concern: our app-level retry policy is aggressive — it retries on 500s with linear backoff but it's still too fast. That multiplied traffic during the transient.
[05:14] Maya: Good catch — that is consistent. Two practical things we can do right away: one, add a temporary circuit-breaker in the integration to cap retries; two, turn on prefix caching for the most common prompt families to reduce KV lookup pressure. Both are config changes, no code deploys.

[07:20] Sofia: We tried toggling caching last night in a small canary and saw lower token counts, but we didn't have a full dataset so it's inconclusive.
[07:30] Jordan: We'll share a specific TTL/eviction suggestion — Maya, can you draft numbers?
[07:35] Maya: Yep, I'll propose per-route TTLs and a tuning doc.

[09:00] Liam: Walk me through the dedicated vs hosted fallback question — Ken (our infra) wants to know if moving to a dedicated pool would have avoided this.
[09:12] Maya: Short answer: dedicated capacity reduces noisy neighbor risks and gives predictable throughput, but it's not a silver bullet if the request fanout and retry amplification remain. In your case, dedicated would reduce contention and provide isolation for KV cache and batch windows. However, your current routing fallback misconfiguration would still have been problematic unless we pin the fallback mappings.
[09:35] Jordan: Also cost tradeoffs — dedicated requires committed capacity. We can model your peak 15-minute burst to estimate cost and a recommended sizing.

[11:40] Amir: On the misrouted fallback, we saw Redwood route to a 7B cheaper variant because the primary node hit concurrency limits. Why did fallback kick prematurely?
[11:53] Maya: Two reasons — our routing threshold was set to try fallback when queue latency exceeded X ms for Y seconds, and because retries created a durable queue buildup, it looked like sustained overload. That threshold was maybe too sensitive for your pattern.
[12:10] Sofia: Is that threshold adjustable in production? Can we relax it?
[12:15] Maya: Yes, it's a runtime flag and we can tune it per-account. We'll propose a more conservative threshold for your traffic profile.

[15:00] Jordan: I want to call out the short-term mitigations we discussed: throttle retries at the integration, enable per-route prefix caching, relax routing threshold, and add an emergency circuit-breaker rule in the console to route to a warm standby instead of cheapest on overload.
[15:18] Amir: For the warm standby, do you mean a pinned model variant?
[15:22] Maya: Exactly — pin a fallback that is compatible and warmed. There's an operational cost but it avoids cold-start amplification.

[18:00] Sofia: For the repro window you mentioned earlier — what does Redwood need from us?
[18:10] Maya: We'll need a dataset sample (anonymized), a traffic replay or synthetic generator that matches your burst profile, and permission to enable debug-level traces for a narrow window. We'll share a secure upload link and an NDA if needed for the dataset mirror.
[18:27] Liam: NDA is fine; we just need to ensure PII is not included. We'll coordinate.

[20:40] Jordan: On security asks — Liam, you flagged wanting SOC2 artifact and audit logs. We have a SOC2 AOC and an audit packaging we can share. Also we can show you per-request audit events in our console for the time range.
[20:55] Liam: Please share the artifact and the retention policy for audit logs. We need to verify retention aligns with our compliance needs.

[23:00] Amir: Back to root cause — Sofia's team captured traces showing a KV miss spike coinciding with a traffic spike and the retry storm. Is the hypothesis that KV miss created repeated recomputation causing longer latency tails?
[23:16] Maya: That's the hypothesis. Miss -> re-gen -> longer operator runtime -> batch windows collapse -> queueing. The caching TTLs and prefetch heuristics affect this flow.
[23:28] Sofia: We also saw client-side retries that don't respect exponential backoff which meant the cluster saw a near-linear increase in concurrent requests.

[25:00] Amir: If we implement the shallow controls immediately, do you think we can avoid another incident before the deeper fixes land?
[25:10] Maya: I think so. The immediate config changes are low risk and should reduce amplification.

[27:50] Jordan: Let's talk about runbook edits — we propose adding explicit thresholds, step-by-step rollback, and a clear 'fall back to warm pinned model' run step. We'll annotate the pages and share a PR for you to review.
[28:06] Sofia: We'll want an explicit checklist for SRE on how to snapshot queue state and when to flip circuit-breakers.
[28:15] Maya: We'll include that — and add a section on how to interpret token-queue metrics vs request-latency metrics.

[31:00] Amir: On longer-term mitigations, what about KV cache sharding or stronger eviction policies?
[31:10] Maya: Those are solid engineering options. Sharding reduces hot-key pressure but requires coordination with your data patterns. We can recommend a phasing plan — quick config tuning first, then sharding and pre-warming strategies next quarter.

[34:20] Liam: Could Redwood run a day-long benchmark simulating our peak traffic and produce a report of expected tail latencies under different configs?
[34:30] Maya: Yes — we offer benching sessions. We'll provision a dedicated capacity mock or run with your traffic shape against hosted variants. Need to align on dataset/legal.
[34:40] Jordan: We'll block 2 hours around Aug 25 for an initial bench, and if that looks good we'll follow with a longer session.

[36:50] Sofia: A couple of nitty-gritty asks: can you provide the exact routing flag names to change and where they live in the console? Our ops team needs them to make quick changes.
[37:02] Maya: Sure — I'll include a config appendix with flag names, console paths, and a one-line CLI for each. Example: routing.fallback.threshold_ms and routing.fallback.duration_s.

[39:00] Amir: Are there any risks with relaxing the fallback threshold? Could that cause a longer blip but less re-routing churn?
[39:10] Maya: The tradeoff is a slightly longer latency before fallback, but with caching and retry throttle that's acceptable. We'll simulate both options in the bench.

[41:25] Jordan: Let's surface the mitigation timeline: immediate (config-only) — within 48 hours; repro & bench — within 7 days; engineering changes (sharding/pre-warm) — next quarter. Does that match your priorities?
[41:38] Liam: Yes. Exec wants cost estimates for the dedicated option as part of the bench output.

[43:05] Sofia: On the repro test, we'll provide request traces and a sanitized sample payload by tomorrow. We need the upload link and instructions.
[43:17] Maya: I'll send the secure upload link and an S3 presign that expires in 48 hours. We'll accept a 10k-row sample.

[45:00] Amir: A question from ops — if we pin a warm standby, does Redwood charge for that continuously even if it's rarely used?
[45:10] Jordan: There is a standby cost — think of it as reserved compute for model warmth. We'll lay out the cost per hour and the cost vs risk tradeoff.

[47:38] Maya: Quick note — there were a few transcript errors in the automatic logs; we've cross-checked traces with the SRE events so we won't rely only on ASR.

[49:00] Jordan: To recap: Jordan sends annotated runbook and routing flag appendix; Maya will run repro with Sofia in a shared window and produce initial logs; Jordan will schedule the 2-hour bench on Aug 25; Maya will propose TTL/eviction defaults and a recommended fallback threshold; Redwood to share SOC2 artifact and audit retention details for Liam.
[49:28] Amir: That sounds good. One more ask — can we get a short one-page summary for our exec? They want the risk, the immediate fixes, and cost delta.
[49:40] Jordan: Yes, we'll produce a one-pager and include bullet cost scenarios for dedicated vs hosted with pinned standby.

[51:00] Liam: Thanks — appreciate the rapid response.
[51:06] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with the action items and links.
[51:12] Sofia: Thanks.
[51:15] Maya: Thanks, bye.
